edits.old: For Macedonian-Australian couples, this is often the custom most changed by distance. If one set of parents lives in Melbourne and the other in Bitola, the asking might be a dinner when both families are in the same city, or a video call followed by a celebration later.

edits.location: Before the wedding > Choosing the kum and kuma, last para
edits.issue: Australian planning tip with an unsourced claim about the Orthodox role; priest advice is already given under the crowning. Cut.
edits.old: For a couple planning from Australia, it helps to confirm early whether your kum and kuma will travel. Their role at an Orthodox service is not one a guest can step into at short notice, so talk to your priest about what is expected of them.

edits.location: Before the wedding > The wedding flag, para 2
edits.issue: Unsourced claim about how Australian families keep the flag. Cut.
edits.old: In Australia, the flag is one of the customs most often kept in a simpler form: carried into the reception, or displayed at the groom's family home on the morning of the wedding.

edits.old: If no one in the family bakes, a local bakery that knows the tradition can usually make one. Bring a photo of a family loaf if you have one.

edits.old: If you are marrying in a Macedonian Orthodox parish in Australia, ask early about any preparation the church asks of couples, what the kum and kuma need to bring, and whether photography is allowed during the service.

edits.issue: Unsourced claim that the welcome 'sometimes moves to the reception venue' in Australia. Cut.
edits.old: In Australia, this moment sometimes moves to the reception venue, with the couple welcomed at the entrance before they go in. If it matters to your family, give it a place in the run sheet rather than leaving it to chance.
